note: The exclusion register (PLAN.md §3). Every tempting parallel that was considered and rejected, with the reason. A catalogue that only records what it accepted cannot be checked; this file is what makes the accepted set falsifiable. Machine candidates that were never plausible are not all listed individually — see `formulaic` batches, which name the shared string and the verses it drew.

categories.wrong-sense: The string matches but the meaning is opposed or unrelated; the parallel is an artifact of English word order.
categories.formulaic: The shared words are KJV connective or narrative boilerplate ('and it came to pass', 'unto them concerning the') that the Book of Mormon uses continuously and that carry no intertextual signal.
categories.common-vocabulary: The shared words are real content words but too widely distributed in the KJV to point at any one verse.
categories.better-source-identified: A genuine link exists at this verse, but to a different source; the rejected candidate is superseded.
categories.insufficient-verbal: A conceptual resemblance with too little verbal contact to adjudicate as a link at any confidence.

exclusions.reason: A four-word run of pure connective tissue. Acts 7:44 concerns the tabernacle's pattern and shares no content word with Nephi's colophon.
Connective boilerplate; Ezekiel's subject is priestly adjudication of controversies.
Four words of connective phrasing spanning a clause boundary in both texts.
Temporal connective. The following noun differs ('year' vs 'hour').

'And/wherefore it came to pass' is the Book of Mormon's single most frequent narrative connective and occurs hundreds of times in the KJV. It should never be treated as evidence of dependence on any particular verse, and candidates resting on it alone are excluded throughout this catalogue without further comment.
A standard KJV formula for prayer with no distinctive content. The real link at this verse is to the Exodus pillar-of-fire theophany; see the accepted link.
Ordinary narrative motion. Absalom's return to his own house has no thematic contact with Lehi's.
Locative boilerplate; the shared string straddles a clause boundary.
A locative phrase. Joshua 10:13 concerns the sun standing still, not a descending figure.
Three content-free words plus 'sun'; Deuteronomy's subject is the hour of the passover sacrifice.
'Filled with' takes wisdom, the Spirit, fury, and much else across the KJV. Hiram of Tyre being filled with craftsman's wisdom is not a source for Lehi being filled with the Spirit.
A stock phrase of prophetic judgement distributed across the KJV; Jeremiah alone offers many closer contexts. Nothing points to Job.
Connective boilerplate spanning a clause boundary.
The shared string is an accident of the Book of Mormon's 'such as' introducing a quotation and Jeremiah's 'such as are for death'. Different constructions entirely.
Boilerplate; Leviticus concerns the meat offering.
Four function words.
Four function words.
Four function words.

A temporal connective. Scored relatively high (1.50) because the five-word run is uncommon, which illustrates that n-gram rarity tracks string frequency and not significance: rare boilerplate is still boilerplate.
Ordinary narrative motion.

This is the most instructive rejection in the chapter. Proverbs 12:10 gave the longest contiguous match in the machine's candidate set for this verse — five words, scoring 2.00 — and it is wrong. The Proverbs verse reads 'the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel': the phrase is there to be negated, and its subject is the opposite of Nephi's. The true source, Psalm 145:9 ('his tender mercies are over all his works'), shares fewer contiguous words and so never surfaced in the n-gram stream at all, but supplies both halves of Nephi's sentence — the subject 'tender mercies' and the predicate 'over all', a pairing found in no other KJV verse. A longer string match is not a better one, and the contiguous-window method is structurally blind to sources whose agreement is split across a clause.

A four-word run of announcement formula. Worth noting for a different reason, however: the 1830 text spells it 'shew', exactly as the KJV does, and the 1920 edition modernized it to 'show'. The orthography is evidence about the Book of Mormon's relation to KJV English generally, and belongs in the variant register rather than here as a link to any particular verse.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that the LORD spake unto
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and worthless. 'And it came to pass that the Lord spake unto' is the Book of Mormon's standard narrative hinge and appears three times in this chapter alone (2:1, 2:2, 2:19); Joshua 1:1 shares it because both texts are King James narrative prose. Recorded here once, at length, as the model case for why n-gram run length is a recall floor and not a ranking (CONVENTIONS.md §9); the same match at 2:2 and 2:19 is passed over in silence.
Connective. Abiathar's banishment shares no content word with the Lord's commendation of Lehi, and the causal 'because thou hast been' is ordinary KJV subordination.
Four words spanning a clause boundary; Numbers 36:2 concerns the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters.

The renunciation list at 2:4 is real, but its Gospel source is the hundredfold saying (Matthew 19:29 and parallels), which supplies houses AND lands AND the promised inheritance. Mark 13:34's householder leaves his house to travel and gives his servants authority — the departure is a parable frame, not a renunciation. Superseded.
Joseph leaves his garment in Potiphar's wife's hand. Shared words are the verb and two pronouns.
Abigail riding down a hill. Pure motion idiom.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when he had
exclusions.reason: Another long run of narrative hinge; see the Joshua 1:1 entry at 2:1. Ezekiel's subject is the man in linen taking fire from between the cherubim.

The Red Sea link in this chapter is carried at 2:5 by the unique phrase 'the shore of the Red sea' (1 Kings 9:26) and at 2:6 by 'three days in the wilderness' (Exodus 15:22). Exodus 10:19, where the west wind casts the locusts into the Red Sea, contributes nothing the geography does not already supply.

Not a machine candidate, but the parallel a reader reaches for first: 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.' The river-and-righteousness figure is Amos's most famous sentence and it is the wrong source here. Lehi's blessing has the wish-formula ('O that thou'), the commandments in the very next verse, and the river and righteousness together — all four of which are Isaiah 48:18 and only two of which are Amos. The decisive fact is external to the wording: Nephi transcribes Isaiah 48 entire at 1 Nephi 20, so the verse Lehi is using is a verse the book will quote.

'Being filled with the fruits of righteousness' shares a participial formula and nothing else. The source of 2:14 is Micah 3:8, the KJV's only verse joining power to the spirit, and it also supplies the prophetic-rebuke setting Philippians lacks.
Four words of which three are function words; the match breaks at 'his wrath' / 'the valley of Lemuel'.
Spans a clause boundary in both texts; 1 Kings 2:29 reports Joab fled to the tabernacle.
Four function words. One of the commonest strings in the KJV.

The senses are opposed, and instructively so. Luke 21:24 is the destruction of Jerusalem: 'they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations.' 1 Nephi 2:20 is the promise that answers that destruction: 'shall be led to a land of promise.' The identical four words carry exile in one text and inheritance in the other, and the passive participle is doing opposite work either side. Worth recording because chapter 1 has already used the KJV's exile vocabulary in earnest at 1:13 ('carried away captive into Babylon'), so a reader tracking that thread has real reason to hear it again here — and should not.

A five-word run and a genuine parallel of form: John 15:10 is also a conditional promise turning on commandment-keeping. But the apodosis decides it. John's is abiding in love; 1 Nephi's is prospering in a land, which is the Deuteronomic conditional of 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7 and becomes the Book of Mormon's covenant formula. The Johannine phrasing is a coincidence of the protasis.

'Cut off' is the Pentateuch's standing penalty formula and occurs scores of times; Leviticus 20:17 is one instance among many. What identifies the source at 2:21 is not 'cut off' but 'from the presence of the Lord', which the KJV has in eight verses and which Genesis 4:16 makes a sentence on a brother.
Four words across a clause boundary. Note that Ezekiel 20 IS relevant to this chapter, but at 2:20 (verses 6 and 15, 'the glory of all lands'), not here.
Jehoshaphat's heart lifted up in the ways of the LORD. The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'the ways of remembrance', which is not a KJV construction at all.

Recorded not as a rejection but as the losing half of a mediation test, because the reasoning is the point. Exodus 2:14 is the ultimate source of the formula behind 'a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren' — but the KJV renders it 'a prince and a judge', and only Acts 7:27 and 7:35 render it 'a ruler and a judge'. The Book of Mormon has 'ruler'. So the Old Testament verse is the source of the story and the New Testament verses are the source of the English, which is exactly what the mediation field 'OT-via-NT' exists to record. Exodus 2:14 is carried in the link's composite list.

exclusions.sharedText: he was exceeding glad for he
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter (rarity 3.00, a six-word run) and the clearest wrong-sense case yet. 'Exceeding glad' occurs in four KJV verses; Luke 23:8 is Herod's gladness at finally getting Jesus in front of him, 'for he was desirous to see him of a long season … and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him' — prurient, and immediately followed by mockery and a gorgeous robe. Lehi's gladness is a father's at a son's obedience. Nothing but the string is shared, and the string is shared because both texts use the KJV's ordinary intensifier. Psalm 21:6 ('thou hast made him exceeding glad with thy countenance', of the blessed king) would be a better source if one were needed; none is.

exclusions.sharedText: go up to the land of
exclusions.reason: Gog's boast about invading unwalled villages. Going up to a land is the KJV's standard idiom of approach, and the noun that follows differs. The same candidate recurs at 3:10 and is passed over there.
Mordecai charging Esther to go in unto the king. Function words plus a verb of entry; the two errands have nothing else in common.
'He would not that any man should know it' — a negated volitional construction, entirely syntactic.

Tempting, because the Joseph cycle is genuinely live in this book (see the Genesis 37:9 link at 3:2) and Genesis 43:5 is brothers refusing to go down to Egypt. But the refusals point opposite ways: Judah's brothers will not go down to face the errand, and Nephi will not go down until the errand is done. The source of 3:15 is the doubled oath formula, which Genesis 43:5 does not have and 2 Kings 2:2 does.
Uriah declining to go down to his house. Four function words around a verb of motion.
'Gold and silver' is one of the KJV's commonest pairs and the Book of Mormon uses it as boilerplate for wealth throughout. Jehoash's plunder of the temple contributes nothing.
'The land of our nativity'; the Book of Mormon has 'the land of our father's inheritance'. The shared span is four function words plus a possessive. Recurs at 3:22 and is passed over there.
'Must needs be' is the KJV's necessity idiom (also Acts 17:3, 1 Corinthians 5:10). Matthew 18:7 is about offences and shares nothing else.

A temporal subordinator from the law of the spreading scab. Note that the 1830 'after that he hath been commanded' was shortened to 'after he hath been' in 1920, which removes the string entirely — the match exists only in the first edition, and only as grammar.
Displaced by Acts 3:21, which supplies the whole clause rather than its opening five function words.

exclusions.sharedText: hath chosen him to be a
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, rarity 2.50, and the object is what breaks it: 2 Timothy's soldier does not entangle himself with the affairs of this life, 'that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.' The Book of Mormon's clause is 'chosen him to be a ruler over you', which is Acts 7:27's noun and Acts 7:35's argument. A good illustration of an n-gram window closing one word before the word that decides the case.

exclusions.sharedText: behold an angel of the Lord
exclusions.reason: 'An angel of the Lord' appears throughout both testaments; the appearance formula carries no signal. Note that Matthew 2 IS relevant to this book, but at 1 Nephi 2:2 (the dream-warning sequence), not here.

'And the LORD came, and stood, and called' — the call of Samuel, and a real parallel of form for a nocturnal divine appearance to a youth. Rejected because the shared words are the two commonest verbs of theophany, and because the content of 3:29 is Acts 7:26-27, which accounts for the whole speech and not just its stage direction.

Solomon's prayer, 'neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel'. The phrase is right and the passage is wrong: the Book of Mormon's ruler-clause belongs to the Exodus 2 / Acts 7 challenge, which supplies the beating, the intervener, and the elder brothers as well as the noun.
The scribes murmuring about publicans. An interrogative formula; Acts 7:26 supplies the same four words together with the situation.

Hushai's counsel, of David: 'thy father is a mighty man'. 'Mighty man' is one of the KJV's stock epithets and points nowhere in particular; the objection at 3:31 is 1 Samuel 17:33's, on sequence rather than wording. Retained in that link's composite list rather than as a source.

Exodus 15:22 is a real source in this book, but at 1 Nephi 2:6 ('three days in the wilderness'), not here. The Red Sea recital of 4:2 is worded out of Hebrews 11:29 (Red sea, dry land, Egyptians, drowned — all four, in order) and 2 Kings 2:8 ('divided hither and thither … on dry ground', a phrase Exodus never uses). The n-gram window caught the noun and missed both.
The man of God to Amaziah about a hundred talents. 'The LORD is able to' is a bare ability-formula; Daniel 3:17 supplies the same words plus the situation.

The Pharisees on Paul's behalf: 'if a spirit or an angel hath spoken to him.' Four words, and angelic speech is common to both testaments. The angel in question at 4:3 is the one from 3:29, whose source is Acts 7:26.
From the law of the slandered bride. Five words, all function words plus a verb of arrival, and the senses could hardly be further apart.
'I said in my heart' is Ecclesiastes' own refrain and a KJV commonplace throughout. It marks interior speech and carries no source.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate at this verse, and instructively wrong. In 1 Kings 13:26 the LORD 'hath delivered him unto the lion' — the delivering is a punishment inflicted ON the disobedient man of God, not a licence granted TO anyone. 1 Nephi 4:11-12 needs the licensing sense, which belongs to the holy-war formula (1 Samuel 17:46, 23:4, Judges 7:9) and above all to 1 Samuel 24:4 and 26:8, where the identical words are used to urge a killing that David refuses. The preposition decides it: 'delivered him unto' is a sentence, 'delivered him into thy hand' is a permission.

Four function words from Esau bringing his venison. Note that Genesis 27 IS a source in this chapter, at 4:21 — the impersonation by garments — which the n-gram stream reached for the wrong reason at the wrong verse.

Elisha barring the door against a king's messenger, 'this son of a murderer hath sent to take away mine head'. A real resemblance of situation — a great man sending to kill a prophet — but four function words is not a case, and 1 Nephi's own Jeremiah frame (1:20, 2:1, 3:13) already accounts for the life-seeking clause.
'It shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it', of God's word. The prospering at 4:14 is the covenant conditional quoted back from 1 Nephi 2:20, whose KJV source is 1 Kings 2:3.
A narrative transition. Four words.

Men defiled by a corpse who could not keep the passover — a six-word run and, on the surface, apt, since Nephi is standing over a corpse discussing the law. But the shared string is a negated modal, the Numbers case is about ritual defilement and not about possessing a text, and the coincidence of setting is the reader's, not the sentence's.

The KJV's one 'hair of the head' is the Nazarite's, shaved at the door of the tabernacle and burned under the peace offering. The phrase is genuinely borrowed — there is nowhere else it could come from — but it is a detail imported into a scene whose source is 1 Samuel 17:51, and it is carried there as a note rather than made a link of its own. Recorded here so that a reader who notices the Nazarite resonance can see it was considered.
The hailstones at Bethhoron. 'Fled from before' is standard KJV rout-language.
The Samaritans asking Jesus to stay. A five-word run of ordinary hospitality idiom; nothing else is shared.

Worth a line because Acts 7 is a demonstrated source elsewhere in this book (2:22, 3:29): here the five shared words are a bare promise-formula, and 7:5's subject is Abraham receiving no inheritance. Not every hit on a genuine source text is a link.

Recorded because it is the single most quotable coincidence in the chapter and a reader will want to know it was checked. 'Plates of brass' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 1 Kings 7:30, the brazen wheels and plates of the bases of Solomon's lavers — so the Book of Mormon's name for its central artifact is, as an English phrase, temple-furniture metalwork from the account of Solomon's temple. It is rejected as a link because there is nothing to argue: the phrase is technical, its KJV context contributes no sense to 1 Nephi, and 'plates' plus 'brass' is what the object would be called in any case. The observation stands on its own and belongs in the register, not in the catalogue.
'The servant of the Lord must not strive.' Four words, three of them function words.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that after we
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run and pure hinge; the 'we' passage of Acts happens to begin its sentences the same way. See the Joshua 1:1 entry at 2:1.

Herod again, at a second verse (see 3:8). Recorded once more only to note that the same wrong candidate recurs wherever the Book of Mormon says a person was exceeding glad, which is often; subsequent hits are passed over in silence.
Hiram the worker in brass 'filled with wisdom'. A filling-formula; Acts 13:52's 'filled with joy' is the nearer sense and is equally generic.

A four-word run and a sharp inversion. 1 Chronicles 20:1 is 'But David tarried at Jerusalem' — the sentence that, in its 2 Samuel 11 form, introduces Bathsheba: the king stays home when he should have gone out, and disaster follows. Lehi says he would have 'tarried at Jerusalem and had perished with my brethren' — staying is death in both, but by opposite mechanisms, and neither text knows about the other.
'I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.' A rejoicing formula; four words.

Rarity 2.00 and entirely spurious: Samson bound with fetters of brass, grinding in the prison house. The 'brass' is the shared word and it belongs to different objects. A clean illustration of a rare-word match with no rare sense behind it.

'The creation of the world' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the phrase is genuinely rare — but Romans 1:20's subject is natural theology and 1 Nephi 5:11's is the table of contents of the Pentateuch. The phrase is doing bibliographic work here and doctrinal work there, and nothing else is shared. Recorded rather than passed over because the rarity count would otherwise look like a case.
'The Lord God of the holy prophets'. The Book of Mormon's holy-prophets formula in this book comes from Acts 3:21 (see 3:20), which supplies 'by the mouth of all' as well.

exclusions.sharedText: which was the son of Jacob
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run, rarity 3.11, and a real observation kept as a note rather than a link. Luke 3:34's 'which was the son of Jacob' is the KJV's genealogical relative, and 1 Nephi 5:14 uses it — in the 1830 wording, which 1920 modernized to 'who'. But Luke 3 contributes only the grammar of a genealogy, not its content; the content of 5:14 is Acts 7:9-14, where Joseph is sold into Egypt and sends for his father and all his kindred. Carried in that link's composite.
'That he might preserve us alive'. The preservation formula at 5:14 is Joseph's own (Genesis 45:7, 50:20), which supplies the famine and the household as well as the verb.
Five function words spanning a clause boundary in both texts.
'Unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ.' Five function words plus a passive; the Book of Mormon's 'it is given in the record which has been kept by my father' is bibliographic.
A negative-temporal adverbial. Paul is disclaiming flattery.

Jacob before Pharaoh on the days of the years of his pilgrimage. A real thematic neighbour — a patriarch's account of his fathers, and this book's tent-dwelling pilgrimage language elsewhere leans on Hebrews 11:9-13, which is Genesis 47:9's New Testament reading — but four function words at this verse is not the place to record it.
'The things of God' is a stock KJV phrase (Matthew 16:23, Romans 15:17, 1 Corinthians 2:11-14). The editorial move at 6:3 is John 21:25's, not Paul's.
Four function words. The verse's source is Galatians 1:10.

exclusions.sharedText: had made an end of prophesying
exclusions.reason: A six-word run whose phrase, 'made an end of prophesying', occurs in exactly one KJV verse — so the rarity is real and the sense is not. 1 Samuel 10:13 is Saul among the prophets in an ecstatic fit, the incident that produces the proverb 'Is Saul also among the prophets?'; the phrase there marks the end of a seizure. Lehi at 7:1 has finished delivering a prophecy about his seed. The Book of Mormon uses 'made an end of' as an ordinary narrative transition dozens of times, which is the better explanation.
A purpose clause. Five function words.
The elders of Moab bringing Balak's words to Balaam. A speech-delivery formula; the following noun differs ('of Balak' / 'of the Lord').

exclusions.sharedText: how is it that ye are
exclusions.reason: Reuel asking his daughters why they are home early. 'How is it that ye …' opens seven KJV verses and is the interrogative frame of Jesus's reproaches at Mark 4:40, 8:21 and Luke 12:56 — which is the register 1 Nephi 7:9-12 is working in, four times over. Recorded as a formula rather than a link because no one of the seven can be identified as the source.
Josiah on the found book. A negated hearkening formula; 2 Kings 22 is a genuine source in this book but at 4:16, where the subject is the recovery of the law itself.
Already excluded at 4:3 for the same five words. The ability formula carries no source; what carries one at 7:12 is the faith condition, which is Mark 9:23's.
'Aaron and his sons did all things which the LORD commanded.' A totality formula.

exclusions.sharedText: say unto you that if ye
exclusions.reason: 'Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised.' A six-word run of announcement-plus-conditional, and both texts issue a warning — but 'behold, I say unto you' is one of the commonest openings in the Gospels and the conditional is bare syntax.
The same Job 42:7 candidate flagged in the chapter 1 pilot as the model of rare-looking boilerplate (CONVENTIONS §9). Still boilerplate.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when I
exclusions.reason: An eight-word hinge. Recurs at 7:18 and is passed over there.

'Judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness.' The Book of Mormon's noun is 'faith', not 'righteousness', and the nearer parallel for a petition answered according to faith is Matthew 9:29, 'According to your faith be it unto you' — itself too generic to catalogue.
Bigthan and Teresh plotting against Ahasuerus. A violence formula; the intercession that follows is Genesis 37:21's.
The apostles reporting back. A six-word run of pure narrative summary. Note that the distinctive word in 1 Nephi 7:21 is 'frankly', which is a KJV hapax at Luke 7:42 and is catalogued there.
Samson's burial. A household formula — and an accidental second hit on Judges 15-16, whose real contact with this chapter is at 7:17-18 and is a different kind of thing entirely.

Stephen quoting Exodus 3:7, 'I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people.' The doubling in Acts is emphatic Hebraism; in 1 Nephi 8:3 it is the accidental result of 'because of the thing which I have seen, I have reason to rejoice.' A window straddling a clause boundary.
Joseph interpreting Pharaoh's dream. Five function words; the Joseph frame in this book is carried elsewhere and does not need this.

'The spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet.' A real generic neighbour — Ezekiel's call is one of the KJV's models for a prophet addressed and moved by a spirit-guide — but five function words is not the evidence for it. The guide-figure at 8:5-6 is catalogued against Ezekiel 40:3-4, where the man appears, stands, and conducts the seer.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that as I
exclusions.reason: An eight-word hinge; Paul on the Damascus road. Note the 1830/1920 divergence at this verse — the first edition's 'as I followed him, and after I had followed him' was cut to 'as I followed him' — so the run is partly an artifact of the first edition's redundancy.

Five function words from the mockers' taunt at Psalm 22:8. The Psalm behind 8:8 is Psalm 51:1, which supplies the whole clause 'according to the multitude of thy tender mercies' and the petition for mercy that governs it.

'The tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it.' Genesis 3 is unquestionably a source in this chapter — but at 8:10, where Genesis 3:6's 'to be desired to make one' is reproduced whole. At 8:13 the shared span is the relative clause and nothing else. Carried in the 8:10 link's composite.

The wedding feast: servants sent to call them that were bidden, 'and they would not come.' A genuinely apt parallel — an invitation to a feast refused — and four common words. Recorded rather than passed over because the parable is the closest thing in the Gospels to what happens at 8:17-18, and a later chapter may find better evidence for it; on this verse there is none.
A negated-volitional formula. Four function words.

exclusions.sharedText: as if it had been a
exclusions.reason: 'As if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam.' A six-word run of pure comparative syntax; the Book of Mormon's completion is 'a world'.

'I am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath.' The rod is the right noun and the wrong rod — a rod of wrath that strikes, against a rod of iron that is held. The four KJV 'rod of iron' verses are catalogued at 8:19; Lamentations is not one of them.
'The end of the world' against 'the end of the rod of iron'. Five function words and a noun that differs. Recurs at 8:30.
Absalom's head caught in the oak. A grasping formula; the irony of a man caught by a tree is the reader's, not the text's.
Nehemiah at the gate of the fountain, by night, surveying walls. Four function words plus a noun.
Cornelius. A vision-report formula; five words.
A causal connective.

exclusions.sharedText: to keep the commandments of the LORD
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run and the single most-repeated formula in the Book of Mormon, used dozens of times per book. Recorded once, here, as the standing exclusion for every subsequent occurrence of 'keep the commandments of the Lord' throughout the corpus; later hits are passed over in silence.
'All these things did Araunah, as a king, give unto the king.' A summary formula.
Lot in the cave. Four function words; the tent formula at 9:1 is catalogued against Genesis 26:17.
Four function words across a clause boundary.
'As we have received a commandment from the Father.' A commandment-receipt formula; the Book of Mormon uses it constantly.
The Levitical service census. 'Ministry' in 1 Nephi 9:4 means the religious as against the political content of a record — a bibliographic sense the KJV never has.

Luke's preface — 'having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order'. Genuinely the nearest thing in the KJV to what 1 Nephi 9 is doing, which is explaining the editorial rationale of a record. But four function words is not evidence, and the sentence at 9:6 is Acts 15:18's. Recorded so the Lukan-preface question stays visible for chapters that may make a better case.

The same five-word run adjudicated as a link at 1 Nephi 1:13, where it is the chapter's decisive datum. Here it is a recollection of that verse rather than a fresh borrowing, and the substance of 10:3 — the return from captivity in the Lord's own due time — is Jeremiah 29:10's.
A narrative transition.
The killing of Athaliah. Five words of temporal subordination; the 1830's 'after that' construction, deleted in 1920, is what makes the run long.
'Both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews.' A pairing formula.

Worth a note rather than a link. 'With one accord' is one of Acts's signature phrases — it occurs eleven times there and almost nowhere else — and 1 Nephi 10:13 uses it of a family migration ('led with one accord, into the land of promise'). Acts 19:29 itself is a mob rushing into a theatre, so the sense is wrong; but the adverb's provenance is Lukan and a reader tracking this book's Acts dependence (2:22, 3:20, 3:29, 5:8, 5:14, 6:4, 9:6, 10:11) should have it recorded.
Already excluded at 3:18 for the same five words.
'Love is the fulfilling of the law' against 'the fulfilling of the word of the Lord'. Four function words and a different genitive.

exclusions.sharedText: come to the knowledge of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, rarity 2.08, and a real pastoral-epistle formula ('come unto the knowledge of the truth', 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Timothy 3:7, Hebrews 10:26). The Book of Mormon's completion is 'of the true Messiah', not 'of the truth'; and the sentence it sits in is Romans 11:24's grafting, which is catalogued at 10:12.
A back-reference formula.
Already excluded at 8:36. Daniel 8:2 supplies the same five words twice in one verse and is no better.
A title plus a copula.
Peter at Cornelius's house. The five words straddle a clause boundary in the Book of Mormon ('by the power of the Holy Ghost, as well in these times, as in times of old').
'What shall be given unto thee? or what shall be done unto thee, thou false tongue?' Five function words in an interrogative; the Book of Mormon's clause is a sign-formula.
'Therefore they were both hanged on a tree.' The shared noun is a gallows. A clean case of a rare-scoring window landing on the one word the two texts have in common and the one sense they do not.

'The form of a man's hand under their wings.' Ezekiel is a real neighbour for the appearance of a spirit-guide in human form (1:26, 'the likeness as the appearance of a man'), but 10:8 is about cherub hands and the five shared words break at the possessive. The verse's link is Exodus 33:11.

exclusions.sharedText: the LORD and he spake unto
exclusions.reason: Hezekiah sick to the death. A six-word run of speech-formula spanning a clause boundary.

The dialogue formula of every vision in scripture, and of this chapter fifteen times over. Revelation 7:14 is where the KJV happens to have it in the same words; it recurs at 11:17 and is passed over there.
Jacob on Joseph, 'Surely he is torn in pieces; and I saw him not since.' Five words of negation. The Joseph cycle is a live source in this book but not here.
Peter's denial, 'I do not know the man.' Five function words, and the sense could hardly be more opposed: Nephi is confessing the limits of knowledge, Peter is lying about it.
The purification of Ahasuerus's maidens. Five words of temporal subordination, long only because of the 1830's 'after that' construction.

exclusions.sharedText: and the angel said unto me
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the standing formula of the angelus interpres. Recurs at 11:26 and throughout 11-14; recorded once here as the standing exclusion for all of them.

The machine's best candidate at the chapter's most important verse, and the wrong one by a single clause. Romans 8:39 has 'the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord' — the right noun phrase and the wrong predicate. Romans 5:5 has 'the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts', which is what 11:22 actually says, and 'shed abroad in our hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. A contiguous-window stream cannot prefer the second over the first, because both share the same four opening words and only the second shares the sense.
Temporal subordination; long only in the 1830, which 1920 shortened.

'Come out from among them, and be ye separate' — a command to the faithful to withdraw. 1 Nephi 11:28 is 'they cast him out from among them', the crowd expelling Christ. Same five words, opposite agent and opposite valuation.
A national designation plus an auxiliary.
Five function words. 1 Samuel 13:6 is cited as a genuine, if weak, source at 3:27; here the overlap is syntax only.

'Judah and Israel were many, as the sand which is by the sea in multitude.' The sand-of-the-sea simile occurs in nine KJV verses (Genesis 32:12, 41:49, 1 Kings 4:20, Psalm 78:27, Isaiah 10:22, Hosea 1:10, Romans 9:27, Hebrews 11:12, Revelation 20:8) and points at no single one. Note in passing that Hebrews 11:12 is the version inside the chapter this book has been quoting since 1 Nephi 2:3.
Four function words.
Genesis 50:17 is a real source in this book, at 1 Nephi 7:20 — the brothers' plea for forgiveness. Here the overlap is a possessive phrase.
David burning the Philistines' abandoned gods. A destruction formula; the chapter's catastrophe vocabulary is Matthew 27:51's and Revelation 16:18-20's.

'The great and dreadful day of the LORD'; Joel 2:31 has 'the great and terrible day of the LORD', which is closer to 1 Nephi's 'the great and terrible judgments of the Lord'. Four function words either way, and 'judgments' is the Book of Mormon's noun, not the KJV's. Malachi 4 is a genuine source later in this book (22:15, 22:24, on Hardy's apparatus); not here.
A standing genitive.
The vision-dialogue formula, five words. Recurs at 12:16 and throughout 11-14; covered by the standing exclusion filed at 11:21.

A demonstrative relative. Note that Revelation 7:14's 'These are they which' is the same construction and IS part of a real link at 12:11 — the difference being that there the whole predicate follows.
'The house of Chloe' against 'the house of Israel'. Five function words.
An assembly formula, used four times in this chapter alone.
Four function words.

Recorded because of the variant rather than the match. The 1830 reads 'the Eternal God, and Jesus Christ, which is the Lamb of God'; the 1920 edition replaced the name with 'the Messiah'. So the four shared words exist only in the first edition, and what they are evidence of is an editorial retreat from putting the name Jesus Christ in a 600 BC vision — the same retreat visible at 11:18, 11:21, 11:32 and 13:40.
'Because of the pride of evil men.' A causal phrase; the pride motif in this chapter is glossed at 12:18 with Romans 1:21's 'vain imaginations'.

exclusions.sharedText: and he saith unto me, these are the
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run of the angelus-interpres formula ('And he saith unto me … These are …'), which chapters 11-14 use dozens of times. Covered by the standing exclusion at 11:21; recorded again only because the run length here is the longest of its kind in the book and would otherwise look like a finding.

exclusions.sharedText: and they went forth out of
exclusions.reason: 'They went forth out of my mouth', of God's declared words. A motion formula. Note that Isaiah 48 is transcribed entire at 1 Nephi 20, so the same words will appear there as a quotation rather than a coincidence.

exclusions.sharedText: and the power of the Lord was
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and pure formula: 'the power of the Lord was present to heal them' against 'the power of the Lord was with them'.

exclusions.sharedText: and he saith unto me the
exclusions.reason: The same angelic dialogue formula. Note that Revelation 17 IS a source in this chapter — at 13:5 and 13:34 — so this is a real source text reached at the wrong verse for the wrong reason.
Temporal subordination, long only in the 1830.
Five function words spanning a clause boundary. The verse's source is Acts 13:10.

'Another book was opened, which is the book of life.' The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'the Book of the Lamb of God', and the KJV's nearest form is Revelation 13:8 and 21:27, 'the book of life of the Lamb' — genuinely close, but five function words is not the evidence for it, and the chapter's Lamb-titles are already catalogued at 11:34 and 13:34.
Five function words.

'Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all' — the right five words attached to the opposite figure. 1 Nephi 13:34's completion is 'of harlots', which is Revelation 17:5's, a KJV singleton, and is catalogued there.

exclusions.sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the earth
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run and a genuine KJV singleton, already adjudicated as a composite element at 1 Nephi 10:12. Its second appearance here is the Book of Mormon reusing its own borrowed phrase for the scattered Jews, not a fresh borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: of the prophets and of the
exclusions.reason: Acts 3:25 is a demonstrated source in this book — at 15:18 and 22:9, on Hardy's apparatus, for the promise to Abraham's seed. Here the six shared words are a bare genitive chain listing two classes of record.
The scribe's assent to the Shema. 1 Timothy 2:5 supplies the same words plus the 'and one X' continuation that 1 Nephi 13:41 has, and is kept in that link's composite.
Five function words around the chapter's governing title.
'That it might be well with them, and with their children for ever.' A Deuteronomic blessing formula; five function words.

exclusions.sharedText: the LORD unto the house of Israel
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and pure address formula. Recurs at 14:26.
Already excluded at 10:16. A back-reference formula.
Already excluded at 10:11.
Already excluded at 13:34 for the same five words. The completion here is 'of abominations', which is Revelation 17:5's.
'The house of God, which is the church of the living God.' Five function words around the noun the chapter is built on.
Solomon's dominion west of the Euphrates. A dominion formula; the verse's sources are Revelation 17:1, 17:15 and 13:7.
Adjudicated as a link at 3:17, where the subject is Jerusalem's destruction. Here it is the same causal formula used twice in one verse and carries nothing.

exclusions.sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the earth
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and the third appearance of a phrase already adjudicated at 10:12 and excluded at 13:39. The Book of Mormon has adopted it as its own formula for the dispersion; repeat hits are not fresh borrowings.

'The wrath of God is revealed from heaven.' The right noun phrase and the wrong verb: 1 Nephi 14:15 and 14:17 both POUR OUT the wrath of God, which is Revelation 16:1's verb and no one else's. See the link at 14:15.

exclusions.sharedText: which are of the house of
exclusions.reason: Already excluded at 12:9. 'The house of Chloe' against 'the house of Israel'.
A closing formula the Book of Mormon uses throughout. The colophon at 14:28-30 — too much seen to write, and what is written is true — is John 21:25's, catalogued at 6:3.

Adjudicated as a link at 2:18 and again at 7:8, where the whole participial clause is reproduced. Here only the noun phrase survives, and six verses later the same chapter switches to the SECOND-person form, which is Matthew 19:8's. Recorded to keep the pronoun distinction visible: 15:4 is narration and takes 'their', 15:10 is address and takes 'your'.
Genesis 50:18 is a real source in this book, at 1 Nephi 7:20 — the brothers falling down before Joseph. Here the five shared words are a speech-introduction.
A reply formula spanning a clause boundary.
Paul's commission. The chapter's Gentile argument is Romans 11:25's, which supplies 'the fulness of the Gentiles' — a KJV singleton — three words later.

exclusions.sharedText: come to the knowledge of the
exclusions.reason: Already excluded at 10:14 for the same six words. Used three times in this one verse, which is why it scores.

exclusions.sharedText: and at that day shall the
exclusions.reason: A temporal formula; the oracle against Edom shares nothing else.
Five function words.

exclusions.sharedText: that it was the word of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of identification-formula. The verse's real borrowing is 'firy darts', four words later, which is a KJV singleton.
Covered by the standing exclusion at 11:21.
Already excluded at 3:18 and 10:13.

exclusions.sharedText: unto you the kingdom of God
exclusions.reason: A six-word run built from 'I say unto you' plus the chapter's governing noun phrase. The exclusion clause at 15:34 is Revelation 21:27's.

'This man was the greatest of all the men of the east' — a superlative of wealth, applied to Job's livestock count. 1 Nephi 15:36's superlative is of gifts, and the KJV verse that ranks gifts is 1 Corinthians 13:13. A clean case of the highest-scoring window landing on the one construction two verses share and none of the sense.

exclusions.sharedText: to keep the commandments of the LORD
exclusions.reason: Covered by the standing exclusion filed at 8:38. A seven-word run of the Book of Mormon's single most repeated formula.

exclusions.sharedText: took one of the daughters of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and the resemblance is genuinely striking at first sight — 'which took one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite to wife' against 'took one of the daughters of Ishmael to wife'. But Nehemiah 7:63 is a genealogical disqualification: the priests who married into Barzillai's family took his name and were struck from the register as unable to prove their descent. 1 Nephi 16:7 is the opposite, a marriage that constitutes a people. The shared string is the KJV's ordinary marriage formula and the two contexts are contradictory.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that on the morrow
exclusions.reason: A nine-word hinge. Numbers 17:8 is Aaron's rod budding.

exclusions.sharedText: in the morning and went forth
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of narrative motion. Jehoshaphat going out to Tekoa.
Solomon's store cities. Five function words plus the chapter's setting.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that as I
exclusions.reason: Already excluded at 8:7. An eight-word hinge, long only because of the 1830's 'that'.
Uzziah's transgression. A standing genitive.
A speech formula.
'He spake many things unto them in parables.' Five function words; the Book of Mormon's completion is 'in the energy of my soul', which is not KJV language at all.
Five function words spanning a clause boundary.
A name collision and nothing more: Genesis 25:16 lists the twelve sons of Abraham's Ishmael. The Book of Mormon's Ishmael is a different man, and the phrase is a bare patronymic.

exclusions.sharedText: up into the top of the mountain
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and a KJV singleton — 'into the top of the mountain' occurs in exactly one verse — so the rarity is real and worth recording. But Numbers 14:40 is the presumptuous ascent AFTER the spies' report, made by men the LORD has just told to turn back, and it ends in slaughter at Hormah. Nephi goes up the mountain under direction from the ball and comes back with food. Same words, and the source's whole point is that going up was forbidden.
Five function words. The chapter uses 'the voice of the Lord' six times as its formula for revelation.

Not a rejection so much as a redirection. The noun phrase alone was adjudicated as a link at 2:18 and 7:8; here it is one of THREE elements of Mark 3:1-5 that this chapter uses, and the link is filed at 17:53, where the command 'Stretch forth thine hand' completes the case. Recorded so a reader tracking the phrase does not think 17:19 was missed.

The Deuteronomic legal triad ('statutes and judgments and commandments') occurs dozens of times. The brothers are claiming Jerusalem kept the law; the formula is doing exactly the work it does in Deuteronomy and identifies no verse.

'The Lord esteemeth all flesh in one' states Acts 10:34's doctrine ('God is no respecter of persons', with Romans 2:11 and Deuteronomy 10:17 behind it) in words the KJV never uses. 'Esteemeth' and 'all flesh in one' are the Book of Mormon's own. Recorded because a reader will want to know the parallel was weighed; there is nothing verbal to catalogue.

'They have become wicked, yea, nearly unto ripeness' and 17:35's 'they were ripe in iniquity' state the doctrine of Genesis 15:16 ('the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full') in Joel 3:13's and Revelation 14:18's harvest image ('the harvest is ripe', 'her grapes are fully ripe'). No single verse is reproduced and the Book of Mormon's fusion — ripeness OF INIQUITY — exists in none of them. The idiom becomes standard in later books and should be adjudicated where it is first argued, not here.

Jeroboam stretching out his hand against the man of God at Bethel, 'and his hand, which he put forth against him, dried up, so that he could not pull it in again to him' — the Old Testament's one withered hand, and a genuine candidate for 17:48's threat. It is carried in the 17:53 link's composite rather than made a source, because the chapter's withering is bound to 'Stretch forth thine hand' at 17:53, which is Mark 3:5's clause, and Mark 3:1 supplies the withered hand in the same episode. Recorded because the Jeroboam scene is the closer match for the THREAT and Mark for the COMMAND, and a reader may reasonably want both.

'They were confounded, and could not contend against me' — the same verb adjudicated at 2:14 against Acts 9:22 and Luke 20:40. Its recurrence here is the Book of Mormon reusing its own formula for a silenced opponent, not a fresh borrowing.
'Our wives and our children should be a prey' — the murmuring at Kadesh. A household formula. Note that Numbers 14 IS live in this book, at 16:30, and is excluded there too.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that on the morrow
exclusions.reason: A nine-word hinge, already excluded at 16:9.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that after we
exclusions.reason: An eight-word hinge, already excluded at 5:1. Worth one line here because Acts 21:1 is a SEA-VOYAGE verse and 1 Nephi 18 is a sea voyage, which makes the coincidence look meaningful; it is not. The chapter's voyage language comes from Mark 4:37-39 and Jonah 1, and Acts 27 — the KJV's real shipwreck narrative — is not in the candidate set at all.
Already excluded at 16:27. A name collision with Abraham's Ishmael.
A standing genitive.

Thirteen KJV verses. The nearest in sense are the Psalter's praise verses (35:28, 44:8, 71:24), which would give 'I did praise him all the day long' a plausible home; none is identifiable and the phrase is too common to catalogue.
'The Egyptians were grieved because of the children of Israel.' A grief formula; the same five words were excluded at 2:18, where the real source (Mark 3:5) supplies the whole clause.

A KJV singleton adjudicated as a flagship link at 2:20 and again at 4:14 and 5:5. Its arrival here — 'we did arrive to the promised land … and we did call it the promised land' — is the fulfilment of the promise made in the borrowed phrase, not a fresh borrowing. Recorded because a reader tracking the phrase will want to see that the catalogue noticed where it lands.

The verse most likely to interest a reader in this chapter, and there is nothing to catalogue. 1 Nephi 18:25's list — cow, ox, ass, horse, goat, wild goat — is a fauna inventory, and the KJV's animal lists (Deuteronomy 14:4-5's clean beasts, Isaiah 32:20's ox and ass) share individual nouns because both texts are naming domestic animals in English. 'Wild goat' appears in Deuteronomy 14:5, 1 Samuel 24:2, Job 39:1 and Psalm 104:18. The list carries no verbal signal, and the historical questions it raises are not this catalogue's business.
Five function words spanning a clause boundary.

exclusions.sharedText: them which are of the house of
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, already excluded at 12:9 and 14:17. 'The house of Chloe' against 'the House of Israel'; the run is long because both texts stack the same function words.
A citation formula, and this chapter uses it repeatedly ('according to the words of Zenock … of Neum … of Zenos').

Herod setting Christ at nought — a genuine parallel, and carried in the 19:7 link's composite rather than made its source. The clause that decides 19:7 is 'trample under their feet', which is Matthew 7:6's and a KJV singleton; 'set at nought' occurs at Luke 23:11 and Acts 4:11 and is the verse's gloss on itself, not its source.

Five words, and the closest single verse for the spitting — but 19:9 has three verbs in sequence (scourge, smite, spit) with an endurance refrain after each, which is Isaiah 50:6's posture and Luke 18:32-33's sequence. Matthew 27:30 supplies one of the three and is carried in composite.
Sinai's pair, reused throughout Revelation (4:5, 8:5, 11:19, 16:18). A theophany formula; the verse's identifiable borrowing is 'vapour', which is Acts 2:19's word for Joel's 'pillars'.
'The four quarters of HEAVEN', in the oracle against Elam. 1 Nephi 19:16 has 'of the earth', which is Revelation 20:8's and a KJV singleton.
Fourth exclusion for the same five words (3:18, 10:13, 15:33).

A standing note rather than an exclusion, filed here so the register accounts for the two chapters it does not otherwise cover. 1 Nephi 20-21 is a continuous transcription of Isaiah 48-49, with the KJV's verse count and versification exactly. Every machine candidate in these chapters is therefore either the Isaiah verse itself — which is adjudicated as a quotation, verse by verse — or a second KJV verse that happens to share Isaiah's wording, which carries no information. No candidate in these two chapters was rejected on judgment; the adjudication is the collation, and the 99 word-level departures are registered individually in data/isaiah-collation.json rather than here.

A two-verse KJV phrase (Esther 10:1, Isaiah 24:15) already carried in the 19:10 link's composite. Its use here and at 22:4 is the Book of Mormon's own formula for the dispersion, established at 19:10 and 19:16, not a fresh borrowing.

Adjudicated at 14:10 and 14:11, where the whole configuration of Revelation 17 is reproduced. Its appearance at 22:14 is one of four previously catalogued sources gathered into that verse; see the link there, whose composite carries it.

exclusions.sharedText: perverted the right ways of the Lord
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and a KJV singleton — and a repetition rather than a new borrowing. Adjudicated at 13:27, where the source verse's 'thou child of the devil' also accounts for 1 Nephi 13:6. Carried in the 22:14 link's composite.

exclusions.sharedText: great shall be the fall of it
exclusions.reason: Third occurrence of a KJV singleton adjudicated at 11:36 and prepared at 8:26. By 22:14 'great shall be the fall of it' has become the Book of Mormon's own formula for the collapse of the abominable church; the borrowing is recorded where it was made.

exclusions.sharedText: the wrath of God shall be poured out
exclusions.reason: Adjudicated at 14:15, where the verb 'poured out' is what selects Revelation's vials over Romans 1:18's revealing. Repetition, not fresh borrowing.

'The kingdom of the Devil' is not a KJV phrase. The KJV has 'his kingdom' of Satan at Matthew 12:26 and Luke 11:18, and 'the kingdom of God' scores of times; the Book of Mormon's antithesis between the two kingdoms is its own construction, and 14:10's 'two churches only' is where the catalogue records the doctrine's shape. Nothing to catalogue here.

'Dwell safely' is a covenant-blessing formula in some fifteen KJV verses (Leviticus 25:18-19, Deuteronomy 12:10, Jeremiah 23:6, 32:37, Ezekiel 34:25-28 and others) and identifies no source. The verse's catalogued borrowing is 'all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people', which is Revelation 14:6's and is adjudicated at 5:18.

Top-ranked machine candidate at 1:1 and 1:2 on a five-word run. 'Deliver ... into the hands of' is KJV narrative boilerplate in scores of verses, and the Amalekite servant's oath to David has nothing to do with a scribe handing a record to his son. Covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusion; listed here only because it topped two consecutive verses and would tempt a reader who trusted the ranking.

'Shall surely come to pass' is prophetic-fulfilment idiom, and the KJV distributes the components widely; 1 Kings 13:32 is a saying against the altar at Bethel and shares no context with Mormon's remark that prophecies of Christ have been fulfilled. The four-word run is the whole of the evidence.

A genuinely tempting candidate: 'hundredth part' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the rarity is maximal and the machine's four-word run is real. But Nehemiah 5:11 is Nehemiah ordering the nobles to restore lands, houses and 'the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil' they had been exacting in usury — a rate of interest, not a fraction of a record. Words of Mormon uses the phrase for the proportion of his people's history Mormon can fit on the plates. Nothing but the arithmetic is shared. Note that the 1830 reads 'a hundredth part' and 1920 'the hundredth part', so the later text moves toward Nehemiah's article and away from Nehemiah's meaning; the change is editorial tidying and not a borrowing. The Book of Mormon's own formula at Jacob 3:13 precedes this verse and is the proximate model; the colophon parallel with John 21:25 is catalogued at 1:5 at low confidence.

'Knoweth all things' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is not the one Words of Mormon 1:7 is using. 1 John 3:20 is pastoral consolation — 'if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things' — where omniscience is a comfort to a self-accusing conscience. Words of Mormon 1:7 means foreknowledge: 'the Lord knoweth all things which is to come', set against 'I do not know all things', in a sentence about a purpose withheld from the writer. That is Acts 15:18's sense, and the Book of Mormon has already fused Acts 15:18 with Deuteronomy 29:29 at 1 Nephi 9:5-6 in exactly this pairing; the proximate model is its own earlier text. The singleton is recorded here so that a later reader who runs the rarity check does not conclude it was missed.

The highest-scoring machine candidate in the chapter (rarity 2.00, five-word run) and the wrong one. 'Come to the knowledge of the truth' is a Pastorals formula shared by 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Timothy 3:7; Words of Mormon 1:8 has 'come to the knowledge of God', which is a different object and a common enough collocation (Proverbs 2:5, Hosea 4:1, Colossians 1:10). The borrowing in this verse is 'delightsome', from Malachi 3:12, which the n-gram stream cannot see because it is one word.

A four-word run with real rarity, and the sense is opposed at the level of horror. Isaiah 9:20 describes famine in a divided Israel: 'they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm'. Words of Mormon 1:13 has King Benjamin fighting 'with the strength of his own arm'. The shared string is an accident of the possessive; the arm is being devoured in one text and swung in the other. The verse's catalogued link is to Hezekiah's 'arm of flesh' speech at 2 Chronicles 32:8, which supplies the antithesis 1:13-14 actually runs on.

exclusions.sharedText: in the land and they did
exclusions.reason: The chapter's longest machine run — six words, rarity 1.20, ranked first at this verse — and worthless, which is the standing lesson about the n-gram stream (CONVENTIONS §9). 1 Kings 14:24 reads 'And there were also sodomites in the land: and they did according to all the abominations of the nations'; the agreement is entirely in the connective seam between two clauses. The real borrowings at 1:17 are 'use sharpness' (2 Corinthians 13:10, a KJV singleton), 'the word of God with' (Acts 4:31, a KJV singleton) and the split 'reign in righteousness' of Isaiah 32:1, none of which the stream ranked first.

'Stiffnecked' occurs in nine KJV verses, seven of them in the Pentateuch's golden-calf and land-possession material, and it is one of the Book of Mormon's most frequent inherited adjectives. Stephen's 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart' is the nearest in rhetorical setting — a prophet rebuking a people — but 'stiffneckedness' is an abstract noun in no KJV verse, and nothing else of Acts 7:51 is present. No source can be identified from the word alone; it belongs in the Index Verborum, not the catalogue.

exclusions.sharedText: with all thy soul, and with all thy strength
exclusions.reason: Recorded so the mediation test is visible in the register and not only in the link. The Shema reaches Words of Mormon 1:18 in the Old Testament's KJV form, not the Gospels'. Deuteronomy 6:5 reads 'with all thy might'; Mark 12:30 and Luke 10:27 read 'with all thy strength' at the same point of the same sentence; Words of Mormon 1:18 has 'the might of his body'. `tools/mediation-check.py` returns one decisive divergence and it favours Deuteronomy. Given how heavily this chapter otherwise draws on the New Testament — Matthew or Mark at 1:15, 2 Peter at 1:16, Acts, Philippians, Revelation and 2 Corinthians elsewhere — the one place it could have taken a Gospel form and did not is worth naming.

exclusions.sharedText: into the hands of their enemies
exclusions.reason: The top-ranked machine candidate for this verse and again for 1:6 and 1:7, with a six-word run. 'Hand of their enemies' occurs in nine KJV verses (Judges 2:14, 2:18, 8:34, 2 Kings 21:14, Nehemiah 9:27, Psalm 106:41-42, Jeremiah 20:5 and others), always in the Deuteronomistic cycle of apostasy and deliverance, and the Book of Mormon uses the phrase continuously from 1 Nephi onward. Nothing selects Judges 2:14 over the rest, and the cycle it belongs to is the book's own narrative default. One entry covers the recurrence at 1:6 and 1:7.

A four-word run of ordinary modal English, and the senses do not touch — Paul says the Corinthians ought to have commended him, Omni says he has not kept the commandments as he ought to have done. 'As I ought' occurs in two KJV verses, Ephesians 6:20 and Colossians 4:4, and both are about speaking boldly, not about failing to keep the law; 2 Corinthians 12:11 is selected only by the auxiliary 'to have'. Recorded because the run is long enough that a careful reader might pause over it.

A tempting case, and the reason the register exists. “did visit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Acts 15:14, James at the Jerusalem council: 'Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.' A KJV singleton matching a Book of Mormon phrase word for word normally carries a link. Here it must not. Acts 15:14 is the KJV's warmest statement of divine visitation as election: God visits in order to take a people for himself. Omni 1:7 reads 'the Lord did visit them in great judgment', where the visitation destroys the more wicked part of the Nephites and the taking-out is what happens to the survivors afterwards ('he did spare the righteous'). The verb is the same and the theology is inverted. 'Visit' in the punitive sense is thoroughly biblical (Exodus 32:34, Jeremiah 6:15, Hosea 8:13, 'I will visit their sins upon them'), so the Book of Mormon's usage is at home in the KJV without needing Acts 15:14 at all — it simply happens to have hit the one verse where the auxiliary matches. Compare the Proverbs 12:10 entry: string match real, sense opposed.

'Hearken unto the voice of the LORD' is the Deuteronomic obedience formula and appears in some thirty KJV verses (Deuteronomy 13:18, 15:5, 28:1-2, 1 Samuel 15:22, Jeremiah 38:20 and many more); Judges 3:4 is one of them and is selected only by the accident of the auxiliary 'would'. Omni uses the formula twice in two verses (1:12, 1:13) as a way of specifying who left with Mosiah, which is a partitive use no biblical verse supplies. Covered here for both.

'And it came to pass that he did according as the Lord had commanded him' is narrative boilerplate the Book of Mormon uses scores of times, and the KJV has the same construction throughout the Pentateuch (Exodus 7:6, 12:28, 39:32, Numbers 20:27) as well as at Job 42:9. The candidate was ranked first for this verse on a five-word run; it identifies nothing. Standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers the class, and this entry is filed only because the run was the chapter's longest.

'Across the great waters' invites Psalm 107:23-30, the KJV's set piece on a sea crossing delivered by the Lord, and the temptation is real because the verse is about a divinely conducted ocean voyage. But 'great waters' occurs in sixteen KJV verses (Psalm 29:3, 77:19, 93:4, Isaiah 43:16, Jeremiah 51:13, Ezekiel 17:5 among them) and the Book of Mormon has adopted it as its standard term for the Atlantic crossing from 1 Nephi 13:12 onward. The catalogued source for this verse's divine conduct is Isaiah 63:12-14, adjudicated at 1:13, whose 'brought them up out of the sea' half is what Omni 1:16 supplies.

A four-word run in a colophon's bookkeeping clause — 'they are written, but not in these plates'. Paul's 'they are written for our admonition' is a statement about the purpose of scripture; Amaleki's is a statement about which plate a genealogy is on. Nothing beyond the words is shared.

'I have seen in the days of king Benjamin' against 'All things have I seen in the days of my vanity'. The candidate ranked first for the verse on a five-word run and is pure connective English; 'in the days of' plus a regnal name is the KJV's ordinary dating formula (Genesis 26:1, Ruth 1:1, Isaiah 1:1, Matthew 2:1). Noted because the fuller run 'seen in the days of' is genuinely uncommon, and because Ecclesiastes 7:15's 'a just man that perisheth' sits close to Omni 1:25's 'a just man before the Lord' — a coincidence of two adjacent verses that could easily be over-read.

'The Holy One of Israel' occurs in thirty KJV verses, twenty-five of them in Isaiah, and is a Book of Mormon fixed title from 1 Nephi 19:14 onward — the book uses it more often than the Bible does. Isaiah 12:6 is selected here only by the length of the surrounding run. Adjudicated at first use in 1 Nephi; later occurrences, including Omni 1:25 and 1:26, are the book using its own formula and are recorded as recurrence, not as fresh borrowing.

A five-word run and the closest KJV parallel to Omni's clause, which makes it worth the entry. 1 Samuel 26:16 is David shouting across the ravine at Abner: 'As the LORD liveth, ye are worthy to die, because ye have not kept your master, the LORD's anointed.' Omni 1:26 is 'as the Lord liveth, ye will be saved'. The oath formula is identical and the sentence it swears is the exact opposite — a death sentence for failing to guard an anointed king against a promise of salvation for coming unto the anointed one. The oath itself ('as the LORD liveth') is one of the commonest formulas in the KJV, some forty verses, so no source is identifiable; but the reversal is worth recording, and it is the reason the Matthew 10:22 link at this verse notes the conversion of a conditional promise into a sworn outcome.

A typological expectation the wording will not bear. Omni 1:27-28 is a party going up into the wilderness 'to return to the land of Nephi … to possess the land of their inheritance', which reads as a return-from-exile and pulls hard toward Jeremiah 30:3 ('I will cause them to return to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it') and Amos 2:10 ('to possess the land of the Amorite'). But 'the land of their inheritance' occurs in no KJV verse at all — it is a Book of Mormon coinage — and 'return to the land' plus 'possess the land' are the two commonest ways the KJV says the thing. Worse, the sense is opposed: the biblical return is commanded by God and succeeds, while Omni's expedition is undertaken by a stiffnecked leader against no divine instruction and ends with all but fifty of them dead. Compare the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry — the typology is pulling, the vocabulary is not.

“strong and mighty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: Psalm 24:8, 'Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle.' A singleton would ordinarily be strong evidence. It cannot be here: the KJV's one bearer of the phrase is the Lord entering his gates in triumph, and Omni's is an unnamed expedition leader whose strength is paired with a stiff neck, who starts a quarrel among his own men, and who gets all but fifty of them killed in the wilderness. Isaiah 28:2's 'a mighty and strong one' inverts the word order and is a destroying storm sent in judgement, which is closer in tone but further in wording. Recorded at length because the rarity count alone would license a link, and should not.

'Stiffnecked' occurs in nine KJV verses — Exodus 32:9, 33:3, 33:5, 34:9, Deuteronomy 9:6, 9:13, 10:16, 2 Chronicles 30:8, and Acts 7:51, which is Stephen quoting the Exodus formula back at the council. Because an Old Testament source here has a New Testament quotation, the verse was put through tools/mediation-check.py against Exodus 33:5 and Acts 7:51: no decisive divergence, because the two share only the single word and the Book of Mormon's surrounding clause matches neither. Every KJV occurrence describes a PEOPLE; Omni 1:28 is the only place in either corpus where one man is called 'a stiffnecked man'. The individualising is the Book of Mormon's own, and no source verse can be identified.

'And I make an end' is the closing formula of four of the five scribal hands in this chapter (1:3, 1:9, 1:11, 1:30) and is the book's own colophon convention, not a borrowing. The KJV's 'neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness' (Ezekiel 20:17) means to destroy utterly; Omni's means to stop writing.

'I, Jarom, write a few words' against Hebrews 13:22's 'I have written a letter unto you in few words' (and Ephesians 3:3's 'as I wrote afore in few words'). The temptation is real: “in few words” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both Pauline apologies for brevity, and Jarom's colophon is doing the same rhetorical work — excusing a short text to readers who might have expected more. But 'a few words' is ordinary English, Jarom's is not the KJV's prepositional idiom, and nothing else in the verse touches Hebrews. The brevity topos is catalogued where it has wording behind it, at 1:14.

exclusions.sharedText: (none — thematic only: the prophets have already revealed what a later writer need not repeat)
exclusions.reason: Hardy's study edition lists Jarom 1:2 in the recurrence chain at 1 Nephi 10:5, whose biblical row is Deuteronomy 18:15-18 — so the apparatus points at this verse for the prophet-like-unto-Moses material, and the question has to be asked. It was: tools/mediation-check.py was run on Jarom 1:2 against Deuteronomy 18:15 and Acts 3:22 and returned no decisive point for either form. Jarom has none of Deuteronomy's 'raise up unto thee a Prophet ... like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken', none of Acts 3:22's 'him shall ye hear in all things', and nothing of Acts 3:23's 'cut off from among the people'. What Jarom 1:2 actually shares with 1 Nephi 10:5 is a theme — 'what could I write more than my fathers have written? For have not they revealed the plan of salvation?' — and 'the plan of salvation' is in no KJV verse at all. The Book of Mormon's Acts 3 form of the Deuteronomy 18 passage is adjudicated at 1 Nephi 22:20; there is nothing of it here to adjudicate.

The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate (rarity 2.00, a five-word run) and worthless. 'It must needs be' is KJV connective idiom (Matthew 18:7, Mark 13:7, Acts 17:3, 2 Samuel 14:14) and a Book of Mormon tic; Matthew 18:7's subject is offences and Jarom's is the size of the plates. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, listed here only because it heads the dossier for this chapter.

exclusions.sharedText: heart / ears / eyes as organs of incapacity
exclusions.reason: Jarom's fourfold catalogue of hardened hearts, deaf ears, blind minds and stiff necks pulls hard toward Isaiah 6:10 and its New Testament citations (Matthew 13:15, Acts 28:27, John 12:40), which is the Bible's standing text for exactly this list. It will not bear the weight. Isaiah's organs are fat, heavy and shut and the New Testament's are gross, dull and closed; Jarom's are hard, deaf, blind and stiff, and not one of Isaiah's or Acts' predicates survives. Worth recording as a trap: tools/mediation-check.py run on Jarom 1:3 against Isaiah 6:10 and Acts 28:27 reports one 'decisive' point favouring Acts — that the Book of Mormon has 'should' where Isaiah has nothing — which is an auxiliary in an unrelated clause and not evidence of anything. The verse's real sources are the three catalogued at 1:3: Mark 3:5, Ephesians 4:18 and Acts 7:51.

Top machine candidate for the verse (rarity 1.50). Romans 9:6 is 'they are not all Israel, which are of Israel'; Jarom is 'they are not all stiffnecked'. The shared string is four function words plus 'all', and the two sentences are doing different work — Paul is narrowing a covenant people, Jarom is excepting part of one from a charge. The verse's catalogued borrowing is 2 Corinthians 13:14.

'The people of Nephi had waxed strong in the land'. “Waxed strong” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (2 Samuel 3:1, Luke 1:80, Luke 2:40) and every one of them has an individual as its subject — David's house, John the Baptist, Jesus — where Jarom's subject is a nation. The KJV's idiom for a people growing strong in a land is Exodus 1:7's 'waxed exceeding mighty', which is the register the chapter is in and which the catalogue reaches at 1:8 through Genesis 47:27. No source is identifiable behind two ordinary words.

A four-word run and a near-miss of the kind that makes the n-gram stream unreliable: Jarom has 'swept them away out of our lands', Acts 24:7 has 'took him away out of our hands'. The agreement ends one letter before it would mean something. Acts 24:7 is Tertullus complaining to Felix that a Roman tribune removed a prisoner from Jewish custody; Jarom is describing the expulsion of an invading army from Nephite territory. Nothing connects the two but the preposition string.

exclusions.sharedText: the arrow / the quiver / the dart / the javelin
exclusions.reason: Jarom's weapon list is tempting on rarity alone: “the dart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (Job 41:26) and 'the quiver' in two (Job 39:23, Isaiah 22:6), so three of Jarom's four items cluster in the whirlwind speeches of Job. But the items are the ordinary furniture of ancient warfare, no syntax is shared, and the sense in Job is opposed: Job 41:26-29 is a catalogue of weapons that fail — 'darts are counted as stubble' — against Leviathan, where Jarom's list is the reason 'they did not prosper against us'. The verse's catalogued borrowing is the craft formula of 2 Chronicles 2:14, into which the weapons are the continuation.

Highest-scoring candidate for the verse (rarity 2.00, two overlapping five-word windows) and superseded. John 15:10's apodosis is 'ye shall abide in my love'; Jarom's is 'ye shall prosper in the land', which is the Nephite land-promise. That promise is adjudicated at its first occurrence, 1 Nephi 2:20, against 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7, and Jarom quotes it as a word already spoken 'unto our fathers' — mediation OT-via-earlier-BoM, not a fresh borrowing from John.

exclusions.sharedText: of the land for they did
exclusions.reason: A six-word window (rarity 1.64) made entirely of function words spanning a clause boundary in both texts — the model case for CONVENTIONS §9's warning that a long run means nothing on its own. Judges 1:32 is the Asherites failing to drive out the Canaanites. The verse's real borrowing, Acts 2:37's “pricked in their heart”, scored nothing in the machine stream at all.

exclusions.sharedText: deliver ... into the hands of my
exclusions.reason: 'I deliver these plates into the hands of my son Omni' against the Amalekite servant's 'nor deliver me into the hands of my master'. 'Into the hands of' is KJV boilerplate in scores of verses and is almost always hostile — delivering a person to an enemy — where Jarom's is a bequest. The colophon's transmission formula has no biblical source; it is the Book of Mormon's own, running from 1 Nephi 6 to Omni 1:1.

'And blessed be the name of my God' is the KJV's standard doxological formula (Job 1:21, Psalm 113:2, Daniel 2:20 for the name; Genesis 14:20 and 1 Samuel 25:32 for the opening). No one verse is in view, and Melchizedek's blessing of Abram shares nothing with a colophon.

The machine's best-scoring candidate for the verse, and the sense is inverted. Job 20:5 is Zophar on the brevity of the wicked man's happiness — 'the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment' — where Enos has 'the joy of the saints' as the substance of a father's teaching. The shared words are an article, a preposition and a noun of the widest possible distribution; the genitive that follows is what carries the meaning, and the two are opposites. The real sources at this verse are Luke 9:44 for the sinking of the words and Proverbs 4:21 for the heart they sink into.

Hardy's apparatus gives this book exactly one Bible row, at Enos 1:4, naming Psalm 95:6 and Psalm 95:11. Psalm 95:6 is accepted as a link at this verse and is plainly right: 'kneel before the LORD our maker' is a KJV singleton and 'our maker' occurs nowhere else in the KJV. Psalm 95:11 is a different matter. Enos 1:4 contains no rest-language of any kind; it is about hunger, kneeling, crying and a raised voice. The psalm's rest surfaces later and twice — 'my soul did rest' at 1:17 and 'the place of my rest' at 1:27 — and both are catalogued there. The row is therefore accounted for rather than rejected: Hardy hangs the whole Psalm 95 contact on the verse where it is clearest to a reader, and this catalogue hangs each half where its wording actually is. The mediation between Psalm 95:11 and its three Hebrews citations could not be decided; tools/mediation-check.py finds no point of divergence that Enos reproduces.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that when i
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, and worth naming only because the content is tempting: Acts 22:17 is Paul at prayer in the temple falling into a trance, which is close to the kind of thing Enos 1:9 reports. But the seven words are entirely the KJV's narrative hinge, the formula covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1, and nothing after 'when I' agrees. Paul is come again to Jerusalem; Enos has heard words in a forest.

Five words, all function words or the commonest of verbs. John 17:8's object is 'the words which thou gavest me'; Enos 1:10's is a land. The verse's genuine borrowing is the retribution clause at its end, 'upon their own heads', which is a KJV singleton at Ezekiel 11:21 and is catalogued as a link.

exclusions.sharedText: that if it were possible they
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the chapter's most seductive false positive. 'There shall arise false Christs' is a KJV singleton and the run 'that if it were possible, they' is nearly one, so the string evidence looks strong. The sense will not carry it. In Matthew the clause is a limit on what deception can achieve — the elect cannot in fact be deceived — and 'if it were possible' is the evangelist's own concessive, marking an impossibility. In Enos it is inside the Lamanites' oath and marks their intention: they would destroy the records if they could. The KJV clause denies the possibility it names; Enos's asserts it. Compare the Proverbs 12:10 entry at 1 Nephi 1:20, the model case for this category.

exclusions.sharedText: girt with a girdle of leather about his loins
exclusions.reason: A real temptation and a wrong one. Enos 1:20's 'a short skin girded about their loins' looks like the KJV's one description of a prophet's dress — Elijah 'an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins', both phrases KJV singletons — and John the Baptist wears the same at Matthew 3:4. But the verse's other clauses settle the source elsewhere. 'Dwelling in tents' is a KJV singleton at Genesis 25:27 and the bow is Genesis 27:3's, so the sentence already holds two singletons from the Esau material, to which Genesis 25:25's 'hairy garment' supplies the skin. The Esau reading also explains why the description is there at all: Enos, son of Jacob, is describing the brother-people. Elijah's girdle explains the clothing and nothing else.

'All manner of' is the KJV's standard distributive and appears well over a hundred times. Numbers 31:30 is the Midianite spoil divided among the Levites; Enos 1:21 is an agricultural inventory. The only content word shared is 'flocks'.

'Hard to be understood' is a KJV singleton, which is exactly why it needs an entry rather than silence. But 2 Peter 3:16 says it of Paul's epistles — writings that the unlearned wrest to their own destruction — while Enos says it of a people: 'the people were a stiff-necked people, hard to understand.' The KJV's difficulty is textual and Enos's is pastoral, and the grammatical construction differs too (passive infinitive against active). Recorded because a careful reader meeting a KJV singleton is entitled to expect it to have been considered.

exclusions.sharedText: of god and all these things
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring machine candidate in the chapter, at 2.33, and worthless. The run spans a clause boundary in both texts: Enos's 'the power of God' ends one item of a list and 'all these things' begins the next sentence, while Luke's 'the kingdom of God' is followed by the promise that all these things shall be added. The verse's real borrowing is four words later — 'great plainness of speech', a KJV singleton at 2 Corinthians 3:12 — which the n-gram stream ranked below this. A clean illustration of CONVENTIONS §9: the stream is a recall floor, not a ranking.

Five words, and the situations are opposed. Habakkuk climbs his watchtower to hear what God will say to him and 'what I shall answer when I am reproved'; he expects a rebuke and is bracing for it. Enos expects a welcome, and what he reports God will say is 'Come unto me ye blessed'. The verse's sources are John 14:2 and Matthew 25:34, both of which supply the speech itself.

'Stand before' God or a king is among the commonest constructions in the KJV. Daniel 11:16 is about the king of the north and says the opposite — 'none shall stand before him' — so even the polarity is wrong.
